title: A hymn in Jaitsri
hookLine: Guru Arjan's Var in Jaitsri opens with a salok: whole at the beginning, the middle and the end

cards: Beginning, middle, end. Somewhere in school, someone wrote those three words on a board and said every story has them. The beginning is full of promise.
The middle sags; it's where people get lost, bored or stuck. The end, if it's a good one, ties things up. A lot of life happens in some middle or other.
Near the end of the Jaitsri section, Guru Arjan begins a Var, a ballad, and its very first salok says something surprising about all three.

teach.h: A VAR: STANZAS WITH SALOKS BEFORE THEM.
teach.b: A Var in the Granth is a ballad made of pauris, stanzas, with saloks, short verses, set before them, like small lamps carried ahead of each stanza. This one, Jaitsri ki Var, is Guru Arjan's, mahala five.
Its opening salok begins: aad pooran, madh pooran, ant pooran, parmesurah. Aad: the beginning.

teach.h: AAD, MADH, ANT: BEGINNING, MIDDLE, END.
teach.b: Madh: the middle. Ant: the end. Pooran: full, whole, complete.
In paraphrase: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end, is the Supreme Lord.
Then: the saints remember the one who pervades everywhere, and Nanak calls that one the destroyer of wrongs, the Lord of the world. Look at the word in the middle. Madh pooran.

Whole in the middle. That's where any story feels least whole: the middle of a long illness, of a degree, of grief, of an ordinary Wednesday. The salok doesn't say God is waiting at the end once you get through.
It says the middle is just as full as the start and the finish. That's where this Var's strength comes from.
Not a burst of courage for the big moment, but a fullness that doesn't thin out halfway, and the Var goes on, stanza by stanza, built on that first promise.
Strength in jaitsri is the strength of the middle.

how: Jaitsri ki Var is sung in kirtan with its saloks and pauris, and its opening salok, aad pooran madh pooran ant pooran, is sung and recited in gurdwaras and at home.

games.q: what does “a hymn in jaitsri” mean?
o: a song for the last day of a long journey
Guru Arjan's Var: whole at the start, middle and end
Guru Ram Das's hymn of a hand on the forehead

games.q: what's inside the salok — tap the pairs.

s: the salok says God waits only at the end
it says whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end.
Jaitsri ki Var is by Guru Arjan
mahala five, a ballad of pauris with saloks set before them.

games.q: you're writing the opening line of a ballad about God and a human life. where do you place the fullness?
o: at the beginning, as the origin.
at the end, as the reward.
at the beginning, the middle and the end.
games.why: Guru Arjan's salok: aad pooran, madh pooran, ant pooran. whole at every point, including the middle, where we feel it least.

practice: Notice the beginning of a breath, cool air coming in, and the end of it, warm air going out, then the small pause at the top where nothing seems to happen, and rest there, breath after breath.
Then think of one thing in your life that's in its middle right now, unfinished, and let it be whole for the length of a breath, with Waheguru in each pause if you pray.

wordCard.voice: A hymn in Jaitsri. Guru Arjan's Var, which opens with a salok: whole at the beginning, whole in the middle, whole at the end. Today's word.
